title: Questions to the Buddha: Kalamas, Tevijja and the Raft
bigQuestion: What kinds of questions do the suttas welcome, which do they set aside, and why?

story.title: The Man Who Wanted the Archer's Name
story.kicker: A man lies wounded with a poisoned arrow and refuses help until his questions are answered.
paragraphs: A monk named Malunkyaputta is sitting alone, the Majjhima Nikaya says, and he is frustrated. The Buddha has never told him whether the world is eternal, whether it is infinite, whether the soul is the same as the body, or what happens to a Buddha after death. He decides to go and demand answers.

He tells the Buddha plainly: answer these questions, or I will give up the monk's life. The Buddha, as the sutta presents him, asks whether he ever promised to answer them. No, Malunkyaputta admits. Did Malunkyaputta ever make answers a condition for joining? No again.

Then the Buddha tells a story. Imagine a man shot with an arrow smeared with poison. His friends bring a surgeon. But the man says: I will not let this arrow be pulled out until I know the name of the man who shot me, his clan, whether he was tall or short, dark or fair, what village he came from, and what kind of bow he used.

That man, the Buddha says, would die before he learned any of it. This chapter reads four famous passages in which people bring questions to the Buddha. Some questions he answers. Some he turns around. Some, like Malunkyaputta's, he sets aside. Each tells us how the suttas think about inquiry.
story.think: Are the wounded man's questions bad questions, or just questions asked at the wrong time? Explain.

lessons.title: Two Young Brahmins
lessons.mainIdea: In the Tevijja Sutta, two young brahmins ask the Buddha which teacher's path leads to union with Brahma.
reading: The *Tevijja Sutta* is Digha Nikaya 13. Rhys Davids translated it in Sacred Books of the East 11 (1881), where he called it On Knowledge of the Vedas. Tevijja means one who knows the three Vedas, the sacred texts of the brahmins. The sutta is set near a village called Manasakata in the kingdom of Kosala.

Two young brahmins, Vasettha and Bharadvaja, are walking and arguing. Each says his own teacher's path is the straight way to union with Brahma, the high god of brahmin teaching. They cannot settle it. They hear that the Buddha is staying nearby and decide to ask him.

Notice the setting. The questioners are not Buddhists. They come from another religious world with its own texts and teachers. The sutta shows the Buddha, as it presents him, engaging their question in their own terms. He does not begin by rejecting *Brahma*. He begins by asking questions of his own.

words.d: Digha Nikaya 13, a dialogue with two young brahmins about union with Brahma
the oldest sacred texts of the brahmin tradition in India
in the Tevijja Sutta, the high god of brahmin teaching whom the young men seek to join

look.title: The Argument on the Road
look.text: Vasettha says that the path taught by the brahmin Pokkharasadi is the straight path to union with Brahma. Bharadvaja says it is the path taught by the brahmin Tarukkha. Neither can convince the other.
look.cite: Tevijja Sutta, Digha Nikaya 13; paraphrased from tr. T.W. Rhys Davids, SBE 11 (1881)
look.prompt: Why might the sutta begin with two people who cannot settle an argument?

check.q: What does 'tevijja' mean?
choices: One who knows the three Vedas
check.why: Tevijja names a brahmin learned in the three Vedas.

check.q: What are Vasettha and Bharadvaja arguing about?
choices: Which teacher's path leads to union with Brahma
check.why: Each claims his teacher's path is the straight way to Brahma.

check.q: Where is the Tevijja Sutta in the Pali Canon?
check.why: The Tevijja Sutta is DN 13.

lessons.title: Blind Men and a Ladder
lessons.mainIdea: The Buddha, in the sutta, uses images of a line of blind men and a ladder to nowhere to ask what the brahmins really know.
reading: The Buddha asks Vasettha a series of questions. Has any brahmin learned in the Vedas seen Brahma face to face? No. Has any of their teachers, or their teachers' teachers, back seven generations? No. Did the ancient seers who made the hymns claim to have seen him? No.

Then, the sutta says, their talk is like a string of blind men, each holding the one in front. The first does not see, the middle does not see, the last does not see. The Buddha adds more images. A man says he loves the most beautiful woman in the land but cannot say who she is. A man builds a *ladder* at a crossroads to climb to a mansion he has never seen.

These images test a claim by asking what it rests on. The sutta's target is not the questioners' sincerity. It is a way of knowing: repeating what one has never checked. Readers often connect this passage to the Kalama Sutta. Hindu readers have their own long tradition of answering such challenges, and the sutta gives only the Buddhist side of the exchange.

words.d: a comparison using 'like' or 'as', such as a line of blind men
in the Tevijja Sutta, an image for a path built toward something never seen
honest belief in what one says

look.title: A String of Blind Men
look.text: The Buddha says the talk of the brahmins is like a line of blind men clinging to one another: the first does not see, the middle one does not see, and the last does not see.
look.cite: Tevijja Sutta, Digha Nikaya 13; paraphrased from tr. T.W. Rhys Davids, SBE 11 (1881)
look.prompt: What exactly does the image criticize: the people, or how their knowledge was passed on?

check.q: What does the Buddha ask first, as the sutta presents him?
choices: Whether any brahmin has seen Brahma face to face
check.why: He asks whether anyone in their line has seen Brahma directly.

check.q: What does the ladder image describe?
choices: A path built toward a mansion never seen
A ladder to the Bodhi tree
check.why: A man builds a ladder at a crossroads to a mansion he has never seen.

check.q: Whose side of the debate does the Tevijja Sutta give?
choices: Only the Buddhist side, as its tellers kept it
check.why: The sutta is a Buddhist text; brahmin traditions have their own answers.

lessons.title: The Path to Brahma Reframed
lessons.mainIdea: The sutta ends with the Buddha describing a path to union with Brahma through four boundless states of love, pity, joy and equanimity.
reading: The Buddha does not leave the young men empty-handed. He asks what Brahma is like. They agree Brahma is free of possessions, free of anger and malice, pure and self-controlled. And the brahmins? They agree the brahmins are not. So how could those unlike Brahma join him?

Then the Buddha, as the sutta presents him, describes a monk who fills the world with love, then pity, then sympathetic joy, then equanimity, in every direction, without limit. Later tradition calls these the four *brahmaviharas*, the divine abidings. Such a person, the sutta says, is like Brahma and can be united with him after death.

Readers take this ending in different ways. Some see the Buddha using the brahmins' own language to point to ethical practice. Some Theravada readers note that elsewhere these states lead to rebirth in Brahma worlds, not to nibbana. Scholars such as Richard Gombrich have argued the sutta plays on brahmin terms with care. The sutta reframes a question rather than simply rejecting it.

words.d: the four divine abidings: loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy and equanimity
to answer a question by changing how it is understood
mudita: gladness at others' good fortune

look.title: Answer or Reframe?
look.text: The young men ask: which teacher's path leads to Brahma? The Buddha, in the sutta, asks what Brahma is like, shows that the teachers are unlike him, and then describes a person whose mind is boundless in love, pity, joy and equanimity.
look.prompt: Did the Buddha answer the question the young men asked? Explain what he did instead.

check.q: What are the brahmaviharas?
choices: Four boundless states: love, compassion, sympathetic joy, equanimity
check.why: The sutta describes filling the world with these four states.

check.q: How does the Buddha show the brahmins are unlike Brahma?
choices: Brahma is free of possessions and anger; the brahmins are not
check.why: The comparison of qualities is the heart of his argument.

check.q: What do some Theravada readers note about these states?
choices: Elsewhere they lead to rebirth in Brahma worlds, not nibbana
check.why: Other suttas link the brahmaviharas to Brahma-world rebirth.

lessons.title: A Town Full of Teachers
lessons.mainIdea: In the Kalama Sutta, people confused by many rival teachers ask the Buddha how to know whom to believe.
reading: The *Kalama Sutta* is in the Anguttara Nikaya, at 3.65 in the usual numbering. Its Pali title is often given as the Kesamutti or Kesaputtiya Sutta, after the town of Kesaputta where the Kalama people lived. It is not in Rhys Davids' SBE 11, so here it is paraphrased from later translations.

The Kalamas tell the Buddha their problem. Many teachers pass through town. Each praises his own teaching and attacks the others. The Kalamas are left in doubt: which of them speaks truth? It is a very modern-sounding problem, which is one reason the sutta is famous today.

The Buddha, as the sutta presents him, first says their doubt is reasonable. It is fitting to doubt, he says, when a matter is uncertain. This short line has become one of the most quoted in modern writing about Buddhism. The next lesson shows what he tells them to do with their *doubt*.

words.d: Anguttara Nikaya 3.65, the Buddha's advice to the Kalama people on whom to believe
the Numerical Discourses, a Pali collection arranged by numbered lists
uncertainty about what is true

look.title: The Kalamas' Problem
look.text: The Kalamas tell the Buddha that various teachers come to their town, each praising his own teaching and running down the others', and they are left uncertain which of them is telling the truth.
look.cite: Kalama Sutta, Anguttara Nikaya 3.65; paraphrased (cf. tr. Bhikkhu Bodhi, The Numerical Discourses of the Buddha, 2012)
look.prompt: Why might this problem feel familiar to people today? Give one example.

check.q: Where is the Kalama Sutta found?
check.why: The Kalama Sutta is AN 3.65.

check.q: What is the Kalamas' problem?
choices: Rival teachers each claim to be right
check.why: Many teachers praise themselves and attack others, leaving the Kalamas in doubt.

check.q: What does the Buddha first say about their doubt?
choices: They should trust the first teacher
It is fitting to doubt when a matter is uncertain
check.why: The sutta has him call their doubt reasonable.

lessons.title: Ten Things Not to Rely On
lessons.mainIdea: The Buddha lists ten grounds that alone are not enough, then tells the Kalamas to judge by whether a teaching leads to harm or to welfare.
reading: The Buddha then lists grounds that, on their own, are not enough. Do not go by repeated hearing, by tradition, by rumor, or by a collection of *scriptures*. Do not go by logic alone, by inference, by reasoning from appearances, or by agreement with a view one already holds. Do not go by a speaker's seeming ability, or because 'this monk is our teacher.'

Instead, the sutta says, when you know for yourselves that certain things are unwholesome, blameworthy, criticized by the wise, and lead to harm and suffering when practiced, abandon them. When you know that things are wholesome and lead to welfare and happiness, take them up. The test is their results in life, checked with the wise.

The Buddha then walks the Kalamas through greed, hatred and delusion. Do these lead to harm? Yes, they agree. And their opposites lead to welfare. So the sutta ends with the Kalamas reaching conclusions the Buddha shares, and taking refuge. The method is *inquiry*, but it is guided inquiry, with a clear direction.

words.d: a text a community treats as sacred
asking questions and testing answers to find out what is true
akusala: harmful, leading to suffering; the opposite of wholesome

look.title: The Test the Sutta Gives
look.text: Not by tradition alone. Not by scripture alone. Not by logic alone. Not because the speaker is your teacher. Instead: does it lead to harm or to welfare, and do the wise praise or blame it? The Kalamas then agree that greed, hatred and delusion lead to harm.
look.prompt: The sutta lists scripture among things not to rely on alone. Is it rejecting scripture? Use the words 'alone' and 'the wise' in your answer.

check.q: Which is one of the grounds the Kalama Sutta says is not enough on its own?
choices: Seeing for oneself that a thing leads to harm
check.why: The sutta names reliance on one's teacher among grounds not sufficient alone.

check.q: What test does the sutta give instead?
choices: Whether a thing leads to harm or welfare, as the wise judge it
check.why: Know for yourselves whether things are wholesome and praised by the wise.

check.q: How does the sutta end?
choices: The Kalamas agree with the Buddha and take refuge
The Kalamas write a new scripture
check.why: After the guided questions, the Kalamas take refuge.

lessons.title: Reading and Over-Reading
lessons.mainIdea: Modern readers sometimes present the Kalama Sutta as permission to believe whatever feels right, a reading many Buddhist teachers call an over-reading.
reading: In the twentieth century, the Kalama Sutta became famous as Buddhism's charter of free inquiry. Books and posters quoted it as saying: believe nothing unless it agrees with your own reason. Some versions circulated online add words the sutta does not contain. This popular reading fits a modern ideal of independent thinking.

Buddhist teachers have pushed back. Bhikkhu Bodhi, in the essay A Look at the Kalama Sutta (1988), notes that the sutta was given to people who were not yet followers, about how to begin. It does not reject faith or the teacher; it gives a starting test and then leads to shared conclusions. Thanissaro Bhikkhu makes a similar point: the test includes the judgment of the wise.

A careful reader holds both. The sutta does invite personal testing, and many Buddhists find that freeing. It also frames that testing within the *wise*, within ethics, and within a path. Over-reading happens when one line is cut from its setting. It is the same danger close reading guards against in the Dhammapada.

words.d: taking more from a text than its words and setting support
a founding statement of rights or principles
in the Kalama Sutta, people whose judgment helps test what is wholesome

look.title: Poster and Text
look.text: A poster: 'Believe nothing, no matter where you read it or who said it, unless it agrees with your own reason and common sense. — the Buddha.' The sutta: do not rely on these grounds alone; know for yourselves what leads to harm or welfare, as the wise judge.
look.prompt: What does the poster keep, and what does it leave out? Name one word from the sutta that the poster drops.

check.q: What do many teachers say the popular 'believe nothing' reading does?
choices: Over-reads the sutta by cutting it from its setting
check.why: Bodhi and others say the popular reading drops the sutta's framing.

check.q: Who wrote A Look at the Kalama Sutta (1988)?
check.why: Bhikkhu Bodhi's essay appeared in 1988.

check.q: What is one feature of the sutta that the popular reading often leaves out?
check.why: The sutta's test includes what the wise praise or blame.

lessons.title: Crossing the River
lessons.mainIdea: In Majjhima Nikaya 22, the Buddha compares his teaching to a raft built for crossing a river, not for carrying afterward.
reading: The *parable* of the raft appears in the Alagaddupama Sutta, Majjhima Nikaya 22, the discourse on the simile of the snake. A man on a journey comes to a great river. The near shore is dangerous. The far shore is safe. There is no boat or bridge. So he gathers grass, sticks and branches and binds them into a raft.

He crosses safely. Then, the Buddha asks, should he lift the raft onto his head and carry it wherever he goes, because it was so useful? The monks answer no. He should leave it on the shore. In the same way, the Buddha says, the teaching is like a raft: for crossing over, not for grasping.

The sutta adds a striking line: the monks should let go even of good teachings, how much more of bad ones. The same sutta warns that grasping a teaching wrongly is like grabbing a snake by the tail. The two images work together. Hold the teaching rightly, and use it for what it is for.

words.d: a short story that teaches a lesson by comparison
in MN 22, an image for the teaching as a means of crossing over
clinging to something; the sutta warns against clinging even to teachings

look.title: The Raft on the Shore
look.text: The Buddha asks whether a man who crossed a river by raft should carry it on his head afterward. The monks say no. He says the Dhamma is like a raft, for crossing over and not for holding on to.
look.cite: Alagaddupama Sutta, Majjhima Nikaya 22; paraphrased (cf. tr. Nanamoli and Bodhi, 1995)
look.prompt: What would it look like, in the parable's terms, to carry the raft on one's head?

check.q: In which sutta does the raft parable appear?
check.why: The raft is in the Alagaddupama Sutta, MN 22.

check.q: What should the man do with the raft after crossing?
check.why: The monks agree he should leave it behind.

check.q: What other image does the same sutta use for grasping a teaching wrongly?
choices: Grabbing a snake by the tail
check.why: Alagaddupama means the simile of the snake.

lessons.title: What the Raft Means
lessons.mainIdea: Buddhist schools read the raft differently: as a warning against clinging to views, or as support for teachings that point beyond words.
reading: Theravada teachers usually read the raft within its sutta. The monks in the story had been misusing teachings to argue or to defend wrong views. The raft reminds them that teachings have a purpose: to reach freedom from suffering. It does not mean teachings are unimportant while one is still crossing.

Mahayana and Zen writers often use the raft more widely. The Diamond Sutra, a Mahayana text, says the teachings should be abandoned like a raft. Zen teachers use related images, such as the finger pointing at the moon: do not mistake the finger for the moon. For them, the raft supports an approach that holds words lightly.

Modern readers sometimes use the raft to argue that any religious practice may be dropped once it feels unneeded. Many teachers across schools reply that the man in the parable is on the far shore when he sets down the raft, not in the middle of the river. The image depends on *timing*.

words.d: a Mahayana sutra on emptiness that also uses the raft image
ditthi: an opinion or belief held about how things are
when something happens; in the raft parable, the raft is left only after crossing

look.title: Three Readers, One Raft
look.text: A Theravada monk: the raft warns against using teachings to win arguments. A Zen teacher: the raft is like a finger pointing at the moon. A modern reader: I can drop practices that no longer help me. A teacher's reply: he dropped the raft on the far shore.
look.prompt: Which detail in the parable does each reader rely on? Answer without deciding who is right.

check.q: Which Mahayana sutra also uses the raft image?
check.why: The Diamond Sutra says teachings should be let go like a raft.

check.q: What detail do many teachers point to against dropping practice too early?
choices: The raft is made of gold
The man leaves the raft only after reaching the far shore
check.why: The parable's timing matters: the raft is left after crossing.

check.q: What Zen image is related to the raft?
choices: A finger pointing at the moon
check.why: Zen teachers say not to mistake the pointing finger for the moon.

lessons.title: The Unanswered Questions
lessons.mainIdea: The suttas list ten questions the Buddha declined to answer, about the world's limits, the soul and the Buddha after death.
reading: The Pali texts list ten questions the Buddha, as they present him, set aside. Is the world eternal, or not? Is it infinite, or not? Is the soul the same as the body, or different? Does a Buddha exist after death, not exist, both, or neither? Scholars call these the *unanswered questions*, avyakata in Pali, meaning undeclared.

The Buddha did not say these questions were foolish. The suttas say he did not declare answers because answering would not lead to calm, insight or nibbana. In some suttas, such as Majjhima Nikaya 72, he explains that none of the four options fits a Buddha after death, as a fire gone out cannot be said to go north or south.

Readers explain the silence in several ways. Some say it is practical: answers would not help. Some say the questions are badly framed, using terms that do not apply. Some philosophers compare it to modern debates about questions that have no answer. The suttas give reasons of both kinds.

words.d: avyakata: ten questions the Buddha, in the suttas, declined to answer
lasting forever, without beginning or end
set up or worded in a certain way

look.title: The Ten Unanswered Questions
rows: About the world in time (eternal or not)
About the world in space (infinite or not)
About soul and body (same or different)
About a Buddha after death (four options)
look.cite: Cula-Malunkya Sutta, Majjhima Nikaya 63; Aggivacchagotta Sutta, Majjhima Nikaya 72
look.prompt: Why might the question about a Buddha after death get four options while the others get two?

check.q: What Pali word names the unanswered questions?
check.why: Avyakata means undeclared or unanswered.

check.q: Why, according to the suttas, did the Buddha not declare answers?
choices: Answers would not lead to calm, insight or nibbana
The questions were in another language
check.why: The suttas give this practical reason.

check.q: What image does MN 72 use for a Buddha after death?
choices: A fire gone out that goes in no direction
check.why: A fire gone out cannot be said to go north, south, east or west.

lessons.title: The Poisoned Arrow
lessons.mainIdea: In Majjhima Nikaya 63, the Buddha compares demanding answers before practice to refusing treatment for a poisoned arrow until the archer is named.
reading: The *poisoned arrow* is told in the Cula-Malunkya Sutta, Majjhima Nikaya 63. Malunkyaputta threatens to leave unless his questions are answered. The Buddha, as the sutta presents him, tells the story of the wounded man who will not be treated until he knows every detail about the archer and the bow.

The Buddha then says what he has declared: suffering, its origin, its cessation and the path. Why these? Because they are connected with the goal and lead to peace. The others are set aside because they do not. So the sutta ties back to the first sermon's four truths. The four truths are the surgeon's work.

Readers point out that the parable does not forbid thinking about big questions. Buddhist philosophers have debated many of them for centuries. What the parable ranks is urgency: first remove the arrow. Inquiry within the tradition, on this reading, has a *priority* order, and suffering comes first.

words.d: the parable in MN 63 of a wounded man who delays treatment to ask questions
what should come first
the monk in MN 63 who demands answers to the unanswered questions

look.title: The Arrow and the Surgeon
look.text: The Buddha says a man struck by a poisoned arrow who refused treatment until he knew the archer's name, clan, height and village, and the kind of bow and string used, would die before learning any of it.
look.cite: Cula-Malunkya Sutta, Majjhima Nikaya 63; paraphrased (cf. tr. Nanamoli and Bodhi, 1995)
look.prompt: In the parable, who is the surgeon, and what is the arrow?

check.q: What does Malunkyaputta threaten to do?
choices: Leave the monk's life unless his questions are answered
check.why: He says he will give up the training unless answered.

check.q: What does the Buddha say he has declared, in MN 63?
choices: Suffering, its origin, its cessation and the path
check.why: He declares the four truths because they lead to the goal.

check.q: What does the parable rank, according to readers?
check.why: The parable puts the ending of suffering first.
